claim: Neuropathic pain remains notoriously difficult to treat despite numerous drug targets.
source: Neuropathic pain remains notoriously difficult to treat despite numerous drug targets.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical challenge of treating neuropathic pain, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Computer simulations predicted that qualitative changes in primary afferent excitability linked to neuropathic pain arise through a switch in spike initiation dynamics when molecular pathologies reach a tipping point (criticality).
source: Computer simulations predicted that qualitative changes in primary afferent excitability linked to neuropathic pain arise through a switch in spike initiation dynamics when molecular pathologies reach a tipping point (criticality), and that this tipping point can be reached via several different molecular pathologies (degeneracy).
evidence: The abstract states that computer simulations made this prediction, which was then tested experimentally.

claim: The tipping point for neuropathic excitability can be reached via several different molecular pathologies (degeneracy).
source: Computer simulations predicted that qualitative changes in primary afferent excitability linked to neuropathic pain arise through a switch in spike initiation dynamics when molecular pathologies reach a tipping point (criticality), and that this tipping point can be reached via several different molecular pathologies (degeneracy).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that simulations predicted degeneracy, which was then experimentally confirmed.

claim: Multiple different manipulations successfully reproduced neuropathic changes in primary afferents from naïve rats.
source: Multiple different manipulations successfully reproduced or reversed neuropathic changes in primary afferents from naïve or nerve-injured rats, respectively, thus confirming the predicted criticality and its degenerate basis.
evidence: The abstract reports experimental results confirming the predictions.

claim: Multiple different manipulations successfully reversed neuropathic changes in primary afferents from nerve-injured rats.
source: Multiple different manipulations successfully reproduced or reversed neuropathic changes in primary afferents from naïve or nerve-injured rats, respectively, thus confirming the predicted criticality and its degenerate basis.
evidence: The abstract reports experimental results confirming the predictions.

claim: Several different molecular pathologies are individually sufficient to cause hyperexcitability.
source: Degeneracy means that several different molecular pathologies are individually sufficient to cause hyperexcitability, and because several such pathologies co-occur after nerve injury, that no single pathology is uniquely necessary.
evidence: The abstract explains the implications of degeneracy based on the experimental findings.

claim: No single molecular pathology is uniquely necessary for hyperexcitability because several pathologies co-occur after nerve injury.
source: Degeneracy means that several different molecular pathologies are individually sufficient to cause hyperexcitability, and because several such pathologies co-occur after nerve injury, that no single pathology is uniquely necessary.
evidence: The abstract explains the implications of degeneracy based on the experimental findings.

claim: Single-target-drugs can be circumvented by maladaptive plasticity in any one of several ion channels.
source: Consequently, single-target-drugs can be circumvented by maladaptive plasticity in any one of several ion channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the degeneracy findings.

claim: Neuropathic pain is pain arising from damage to or dysfunction of the nervous system.
source: Neuropathic pain—pain arising from damage to or dysfunction of the nervous system (Merskey and Bogduk, 1994)—is notoriously difficult to treat.
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claim: Effective treatments for neuropathic pain have eluded discovery despite intense research and many promising leads.
source: Effective treatments have eluded discovery despite intense research and many promising leads (Woolf, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Proposed explanations for the lack of clinical translation have focused on preclinical animal models and on clinical trial design.
source: Proposed explanations for the lack of clinical translation have focused on preclinical animal models (Rice et al., 2008; Mogil, 2009) and on clinical trial design (Dworkin et al., 2011; Mao, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Degeneracy within the pain system may allow the pathogenic process to circumvent single-target-drugs.
source: An alternative possibility is that degeneracy within the pain system allows the pathogenic process to circumvent single-target-drugs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: If degeneracy allows the pathogenic process to circumvent single-target-drugs, the single-target-drug paradigm is bound to fail no matter how good the animal models or clinical trials are.
source: If true, the single-target-drug paradigm is bound to fail no matter how good the animal models or clinical trials are, and a new paradigm is needed.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the degeneracy hypothesis.

claim: Degeneracy refers to multiple 'different' mechanisms conveying equivalent function.
source: Degeneracy refers to multiple 'different' mechanisms conveying equivalent function (Edelman and Gally, 2001); by comparison, redundancy refers to multiple instantiations of the 'same' mechanism.
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claim: Redundancy refers to multiple instantiations of the 'same' mechanism.
source: Degeneracy refers to multiple 'different' mechanisms conveying equivalent function (Edelman and Gally, 2001); by comparison, redundancy refers to multiple instantiations of the 'same' mechanism.
evidence: This is a definition provided for comparison with degeneracy.

claim: Both degeneracy and redundancy convey robustness to complex systems.
source: Both convey robustness to complex systems (Kitano, 2004a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: If a pathogenic process were to hijack degeneracy, the pathological state could itself become robust, or resistant to treatment.
source: But if a pathogenic process were to hijack degeneracy, the pathological state could itself become robust, or in other words resistant to treatment.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of degeneracy in pathological states.

claim: Degeneracy is recognized as an important factor for cancer and other complex diseases.
source: Accordingly, degeneracy is recognized as an important factor for cancer and other complex diseases (Kitano, 2004a, 2004b; Tian et al., 2011), including epilepsy (Klassen et al., 2011) but has yet to inform pain research or analgesic drug development.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Degeneracy is recognized as an important factor for epilepsy.
source: Accordingly, degeneracy is recognized as an important factor for cancer and other complex diseases (Kitano, 2004a, 2004b; Tian et al., 2011), including epilepsy (Klassen et al., 2011) but has yet to inform pain research or analgesic drug development.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Degeneracy has yet to inform pain research or analgesic drug development.
source: Accordingly, degeneracy is recognized as an important factor for cancer and other complex diseases (Kitano, 2004a, 2004b; Tian et al., 2011), including epilepsy (Klassen et al., 2011) but has yet to inform pain research or analgesic drug development.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of pain research.

claim: Degeneracy has been recognized in neural systems.
source: That said, degeneracy has been recognized in neural systems (Prinz et al., 2004) and its existence and functional implications are gaining increasing attention (Grashow et al., 2009, 2010; Marder, 2011; Amendola et al., 2012; Zhao and Golowasch, 2012; Gutierrez et al., 2013; O'Leary et al., 2013; Ransdell et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Increased function of the sodium channel Nav1.8 is sufficient to produce the hypersensitivity associated with neuropathic pain.
source: For example, increased function of the sodium channel Nav1.8 is sufficient to produce the hypersensitivity associated with neuropathic pain (Bierhaus et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Nav1.8-targetted manipulations predictably fail in Nav1.8 knock-out animals.
source: Nav1.8-targetted manipulations predictably fail in Nav1.8 knock-out animals, but those animals can nonetheless develop injury-induced hypersensitivity (Nassar et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Nav1.8 knock-out animals can nonetheless develop injury-induced hypersensitivity.
source: Nav1.8-targetted manipulations predictably fail in Nav1.8 knock-out animals, but those animals can nonetheless develop injury-induced hypersensitivity (Nassar et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Injury-induced changes in other ion channels are also sufficient to cause neuropathic pain.
source: This indicates that injury-induced changes in other ion channels—and indeed many such changes occur (for reviews, see Campbell and Meyer, 2006; Woolf and Ma, 2007; Basbaum et al., 2009; Marchand et al., 2009; Gold and Gebhart, 2010)—are also sufficient to cause neuropathic pain.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Many injury-induced changes in ion channels occur after nerve injury.
source: This indicates that injury-induced changes in other ion channels—and indeed many such changes occur (for reviews, see Campbell and Meyer, 2006; Woolf and Ma, 2007; Basbaum et al., 2009; Marchand et al., 2009; Gold and Gebhart, 2010)—are also sufficient to cause neuropathic pain.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Hyperexcitability develops at multiple points along the neuraxis.
source: Hyperexcitability characterized by quantitative changes such as reduced threshold and qualitative changes such as altered spiking patterns (see below) develops at multiple points along the neuraxis (Costigan et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Hyperexcitability is characterized by quantitative changes such as reduced threshold.
source: Hyperexcitability characterized by quantitative changes such as reduced threshold and qualitative changes such as altered spiking patterns (see below) develops at multiple points along the neuraxis (Costigan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of hyperexcitability supported by a citation.

claim: Hyperexcitability is characterized by qualitative changes such as altered spiking patterns.
source: Hyperexcitability characterized by quantitative changes such as reduced threshold and qualitative changes such as altered spiking patterns (see below) develops at multiple points along the neuraxis (Costigan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of hyperexcitability supported by a citation.

claim: Spontaneous spiking and exaggerated responsiveness of primary somatosensory afferents are thought to underlie spontaneous pain and hypersensitivity, respectively.
source: This includes primary somatosensory afferents whose spontaneous spiking and exaggerated responsiveness are thought to underlie spontaneous pain and hypersensitivity, respectively (for review, see Devor, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Peripheral input helps drive central sensitization.
source: Notably, peripheral input helps drive central sensitization (Devor, 1991; Gracely et al., 1992; Koltzenburg et al., 1994), meaning increased peripheral input is amplified rather than attenuated centrally.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Increased peripheral input is amplified rather than attenuated centrally.
source: Notably, peripheral input helps drive central sensitization (Devor, 1991; Gracely et al., 1992; Koltzenburg et al., 1994), meaning increased peripheral input is amplified rather than attenuated centrally.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited studies on central sensitization.

claim: Injury-induced hyperexcitability is not limited to nociceptors.
source: Injury-induced hyperexcitability is not limited to nociceptors; on the contrary, hyperexcitability also develops in myelinated afferents that normally convey innocuous information but that contribute to mechanical allodynia (hypersensitivity) under neuropathic conditions (Campbell et al., 1988; Koltzenburg et al., 1994; Devor, 2009; King et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hyperexcitability develops in myelinated afferents that normally convey innocuous information but that contribute to mechanical allodynia under neuropathic conditions.
source: Injury-induced hyperexcitability is not limited to nociceptors; on the contrary, hyperexcitability also develops in myelinated afferents that normally convey innocuous information but that contribute to mechanical allodynia (hypersensitivity) under neuropathic conditions (Campbell et al., 1988; Koltzenburg et al., 1994; Devor, 2009; King et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hyperexcitability in myelinated afferents is characterized by a triad of qualitative changes that include repetitive spiking, membrane potential oscillations (MPOs), and bursting.
source: Hyperexcitability in myelinated afferents is characterized by a triad of qualitative changes that include repetitive spiking, membrane potential oscillations (MPOs), and bursting (Liu et al., 2000; Herzog et al., 2001; Xing et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2002; Ma and LaMotte, 2007; Fan et al., 2011; Xie et al., 2011; Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: All three neuropathic changes (repetitive spiking, MPOs, and bursting) arise from a switch in spike initiation dynamics.
source: We recently showed through mathematical modeling that all three neuropathic changes arise from a switch in spike initiation dynamics (Rho and Prescott, 2012); there is, therefore, a one-to-many mapping between altered spike initiation dynamics and qualitative changes in cellular excitability.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the authors' previous modeling work.

claim: There is a one-to-many mapping between altered spike initiation dynamics and qualitative changes in cellular excitability.
source: We recently showed through mathematical modeling that all three neuropathic changes arise from a switch in spike initiation dynamics (Rho and Prescott, 2012); there is, therefore, a one-to-many mapping between altered spike initiation dynamics and qualitative changes in cellular excitability.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: There is a many-to-one mapping between parameter values (whose variations represent injury-induced molecular changes) and cellular excitability.
source: On the other hand, we found a many-to-one mapping between parameter values (whose variations represent injury-induced molecular changes) and cellular excitability; moreover, continuous parameter variations led to a discontinuous change in spike initiation dynamics.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' modeling work.

claim: Continuous parameter variations led to a discontinuous change in spike initiation dynamics.
source: On the other hand, we found a many-to-one mapping between parameter values (whose variations represent injury-induced molecular changes) and cellular excitability; moreover, continuous parameter variations led to a discontinuous change in spike initiation dynamics.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' modeling work.

claim: The many-to-one mapping constitutes degeneracy.
source: The many-to-one mapping constitutes degeneracy and the discontinuity, or tipping point, reflects criticality.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: The discontinuity, or tipping point, reflects criticality.
source: The many-to-one mapping constitutes degeneracy and the discontinuity, or tipping point, reflects criticality.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Spike initiation is a key nonlinear process whose qualitative alteration explains multiple features of cellular hyperexcitability on the basis of several possible molecular pathologies.
source: The results identify spike initiation as a key nonlinear process whose qualitative alteration explains multiple features of cellular hyperexcitability on the basis of several possible molecular pathologies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling work.

claim: Spike initiation occurs through a time- and voltage-dependent competition between net fast-activating inward current and net slower-activating outward current.
source: According to our previous theoretical work, spike initiation occurs through a time- and voltage-dependent competition between net fast-activating inward current and net slower-activating outward current (Prescott et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Multiple types of ion channels contribute to each net current.
source: Because multiple types of ion channels contribute to each net current—currents with similar kinetics sum linearly (Kepler et al., 1992)—injury-induced changes in any one of the contributing ion channels can bias the competition (Rho and Prescott, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Currents with similar kinetics sum linearly.
source: Because multiple types of ion channels contribute to each net current—currents with similar kinetics sum linearly (Kepler et al., 1992)—injury-induced changes in any one of the contributing ion channels can bias the competition (Rho and Prescott, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Injury-induced changes in any one of the contributing ion channels can bias the competition between inward and outward currents.
source: Because multiple types of ion channels contribute to each net current—currents with similar kinetics sum linearly (Kepler et al., 1992)—injury-induced changes in any one of the contributing ion channels can bias the competition (Rho and Prescott, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The spike threshold in the soma of myelinated afferents is about −35 mV.
source: Using a Morris–Lecar model that comprises only two variables whose interaction is sufficient to produce spikes, we adjusted parameters ('Materials and methods') to give a spike threshold approximating that observed in the soma of myelinated afferents, which is about −35 mV.
evidence: This is a parameter used in the modeling based on experimental observations.

claim: Somata of myelinated primary afferents normally generate a single spike at stimulus onset.
source: Somata of myelinated primary afferents normally generate a single spike at stimulus onset, which corresponds to the gray-shaded region, whereas a subset of those neurons spike repetitively after nerve injury (e.g., Liu et al., 2002), which corresponds to the colored region.
evidence: This statement describes normal neuronal behavior and is supported by a citation for the injury condition.

claim: A subset of myelinated primary afferents spike repetitively after nerve injury.
source: Somata of myelinated primary afferents normally generate a single spike at stimulus onset, which corresponds to the gray-shaded region, whereas a subset of those neurons spike repetitively after nerve injury (e.g., Liu et al., 2002), which corresponds to the colored region.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Neuropathic changes in excitability arise from a switch in spike initiation dynamics.
source: Neuropathic changes in excitability arise from a switch in spike initiation dynamics (Rho and Prescott, 2012; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: A subcritical Hopf bifurcation occurs in the neuropathic parameter regime when stimulus intensity reaches a critical value.
source: In brief, the colored region of Figure 1B corresponds to a parameter regime in which a subcritical Hopf bifurcation occurs when stimulus intensity Istim reaches a critical value I*.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling results shown in the figure.

claim: Repetitive spiking occurs when stimulus intensity exceeds the critical value I*.
source: A Hopf bifurcation represents destabilization of the 'resting' state: repetitive spiking occurs when Istim exceeds I*, membrane potential oscillations (MPOs) arise in the presence of noise when Istim approaches I*, and bursting occurs when adaptation Iadapt causes Istim−Iadapt to sweep back and forth across I*.
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling results.

claim: Membrane potential oscillations (MPOs) arise in the presence of noise when stimulus intensity approaches the critical value I*.
source: A Hopf bifurcation represents destabilization of the 'resting' state: repetitive spiking occurs when Istim exceeds I*, membrane potential oscillations (MPOs) arise in the presence of noise when Istim approaches I*, and bursting occurs when adaptation Iadapt causes Istim−Iadapt to sweep back and forth across I*.
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling results.

claim: Bursting occurs when adaptation causes stimulus intensity minus adaptation to sweep back and forth across the critical value I*.
source: A Hopf bifurcation represents destabilization of the 'resting' state: repetitive spiking occurs when Istim exceeds I*, membrane potential oscillations (MPOs) arise in the presence of noise when Istim approaches I*, and bursting occurs when adaptation Iadapt causes Istim−Iadapt to sweep back and forth across I*.
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling results.

claim: Outside the neuropathic parameter regime, spike initiation is effectively limited to a quasi-separatrix crossing.
source: Outside the colored region of Figure 1B, spike initiation is effectively limited to a quasi-separatrix crossing; according to this mechanism, the resting state remains stable but a single spike is produced if the system transiently escapes from that state during a stimulus transient.
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling results.

claim: In the absence of a Hopf bifurcation, repetitive spiking, MPOs and bursting are simply not possible.
source: In the absence of a Hopf bifurcation, repetitive spiking, MPOs and bursting are simply not possible.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the dynamical analysis.

claim: A cell with normal excitability can be converted to neuropathic excitability by a decrease in potassium conductance.
source: We predict that a cell with normal excitability can be converted to neuropathic excitability (i.e., forced across its tipping point) by a decrease in ḡK, an increase in ḡNa, or some combination thereof (arrows 1–3 on Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the modeling.

claim: A cell with normal excitability can be converted to neuropathic excitability by an increase in sodium conductance.
source: We predict that a cell with normal excitability can be converted to neuropathic excitability (i.e., forced across its tipping point) by a decrease in ḡK, an increase in ḡNa, or some combination thereof (arrows 1–3 on Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the modeling.

claim: A cell with normal excitability can be converted to neuropathic excitability by some combination of decreased potassium conductance and increased sodium conductance.
source: We predict that a cell with normal excitability can be converted to neuropathic excitability (i.e., forced across its tipping point) by a decrease in ḡK, an increase in ḡNa, or some combination thereof (arrows 1–3 on Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the modeling.

claim: Balanced conductance changes may offset one another, resulting in no qualitative alteration of excitability.
source: However, balanced conductance changes may offset one another, resulting in no qualitative alteration of excitability (arrow 4).
evidence: This is a prediction from the modeling.

claim: Inverse changes to those that produce neuropathic excitability are predicted to normalize excitability in a hyperexcitable cell.
source: Contrariwise, the inverse changes are predicted to normalize excitability in a hyperexcitable cell by forcing the system in the opposite direction across its tipping point (arrows 5 and 6).
evidence: This is a prediction from the modeling.

claim: Changes in other conductances, in parameters other than maximal conductance, or in parameters not strictly connected to conductance can all affect where the tipping point lies.
source: Changes in other conductances, in parameters other than maximal conductance (e.g., activation properties), or in parameters not strictly connected to conductance (e.g., reversal potential) can all affect where the tipping point lies (Figure 1D–F, respectively).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: The tipping point in a real neuron will depend on numerous parameters and thus correspond to a boundary within a high-dimensional space.
source: But one should bear in mind that the tipping point in a real neuron will depend on numerous parameters and thus correspond to a boundary within a high-dimensional space.
evidence: This is an inference about the complexity of real neurons based on the modeling.

claim: Excitability can change abruptly on the basis of many different molecular changes when those molecular changes reach a tipping point.
source: In other words, our theory predicts that excitability can change abruptly on the basis of many different molecular changes when and if those molecular changes reach a tipping point.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical predictions.

claim: Myelinated afferents are directly implicated in allodynia.
source: We targeted myelinated afferents (somatic diameter ≥30 µm) because they are directly implicated in allodynia and because they have been reported to develop the triad of neuropathic excitability changes described in the 'Introduction'.
evidence: This is a rationale for the experimental approach based on established knowledge.

claim: Myelinated afferents have been reported to develop the triad of neuropathic excitability changes (repetitive spiking, MPOs, and bursting).
source: We targeted myelinated afferents (somatic diameter ≥30 µm) because they are directly implicated in allodynia and because they have been reported to develop the triad of neuropathic excitability changes described in the 'Introduction'.
evidence: This is a rationale for the experimental approach based on previous reports.

claim: Neurons harvested from naive, uninjured rats responded to a square pulse of current injection with onset-only spiking, even at high stimulus intensities.
source: In keeping with previous studies, neurons harvested from naive, uninjured rats responded to a square pulse of current injection with onset-only spiking, even at high stimulus intensities (Figure 2A; n = 23 cutaneous afferents).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Neurons could spike again in response to subsequent increments in stimulus intensity, ruling out complete sodium channel inactivation as the basis for non-repetitive spiking.
source: Neurons could spike again in response to subsequent increments in stimulus intensity (Figure 2A, inset), thus ruling out complete sodium channel inactivation as the basis for non-repetitive spiking.
evidence: This is an experimental observation and interpretation.

claim: Decreasing subthreshold potassium conductance would reproduce neuropathic changes in excitability, consistent with injury-induced reduction of Kv1 channels.
source: Our first prediction was that decreasing subthreshold potassium conductance would reproduce neuropathic changes in excitability, consistent with injury-induced reduction of Kv1 channels (Everill and Kocsis, 1999; Ishikawa et al., 1999; Kim et al., 2002; Hammer et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a prediction supported by citations to studies showing injury-induced reduction of Kv1 channels.

claim: As 4-AP concentration increased during wash-in, MPOs developed followed by a switch to repetitive spiking during stimulation.
source: As drug concentration increased during wash-in, MPOs developed followed by a switch to repetitive spiking during stimulation; the reverse sequence occurred during washout (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The reverse sequence (repetitive spiking followed by MPOs) occurred during 4-AP washout.
source: As drug concentration increased during wash-in, MPOs developed followed by a switch to repetitive spiking during stimulation; the reverse sequence occurred during washout (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Pharmacologically induced MPOs are consistent with previous descriptions of injury-induced MPOs.
source: The broad peak in the power spectrum (Figure 2B, inset) shows that pharmacologically induced MPOs are consistent with previous descriptions of injury-induced MPOs (Song et al., 2012) and with a noise-dependent mechanism (Rho and Prescott, 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results with previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Pharmacologically induced MPOs are consistent with a noise-dependent mechanism.
source: The broad peak in the power spectrum (Figure 2B, inset) shows that pharmacologically induced MPOs are consistent with previous descriptions of injury-induced MPOs (Song et al., 2012) and with a noise-dependent mechanism (Rho and Prescott, 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results with theoretical predictions, supported by a citation.

claim: In 6 of 11 neurons tested, MPOs and repetitive spiking co-developed during wash-in of 4-AP.
source: In 6 of 11 neurons tested, MPOs and repetitive spiking co-developed during wash-in of 4-AP, consistent with their common connection with the subcritical Hopf bifurcation.
evidence: This is an experimental result.

claim: Co-development of MPOs and repetitive spiking is consistent with their common connection with the subcritical Hopf bifurcation.
source: In 6 of 11 neurons tested, MPOs and repetitive spiking co-developed during wash-in of 4-AP, consistent with their common connection with the subcritical Hopf bifurcation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on the theoretical model.

claim: Bursting was not observed with 4-AP application alone.
source: Bursting was not observed (see below).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Using 5 nM α-dendrotoxin, which more selectively blocks Kv1 channels, equivalent results were obtained in 2 of 4 additional neurons.
source: Using 5 nM α-dendrotoxin, which more selectively blocks Kv1 channels, we obtained equivalent results in 2 of 4 additional neurons (data not shown).
evidence: This is an experimental result.

claim: Reproduction of neuropathic excitability via potassium channel blockade in 8 of 15 neurons represents a significantly higher conversion rate than expected by chance.
source: Reproduction of neuropathic excitability via potassium channel blockade in a total of 8 of 15 neurons represents a significantly higher conversion rate than expected by chance (i.e., 0 of 23 neurons, as determined from the excitability at the start and end of recordings in each neuron; p<0.001; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental results.

claim: Increasing subthreshold sodium conductance would reproduce neuropathic excitability, consistent with injury-induced increase of Nav1.3.
source: Our second prediction was that increasing subthreshold sodium conductance would reproduce neuropathic excitability, consistent with injury-induced increase of Nav1.3 (Waxman et al., 1994; Kim et al., 2001; Fukuoka et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a prediction supported by citations to studies showing injury-induced increase of Nav1.3.

claim: Increasing the virtual sodium current produced MPOs and repetitive spiking.
source: As expected, increasing the virtual sodium current produced MPOs and repetitive spiking (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Dynamic clamp-induced MPOs are comparable to injury- and pharmacologically-induced MPOs.
source: Power spectral analysis (Figure 2C, inset) shows that dynamic clamp-induced MPOs are comparable to injury- and pharmacologically-induced MPOs.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results.

claim: In 9 of 19 neurons tested, MPOs and repetitive spiking co-developed when sufficient virtual sodium conductance was inserted.
source: In 9 of 19 neurons tested, MPOs and repetitive spiking co-developed when sufficient virtual sodium conductance was inserted; this conversion rate is significantly higher than expected by chance (p<0.001; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Of the 10 neurons that did not develop repetitive spiking with virtual sodium conductance, five nonetheless developed MPOs.
source: Of the 10 neurons that did not develop repetitive spiking, five nonetheless developed MPOs.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Bursting requires a subcritical Hopf bifurcation and adaptation.
source: Our modeling indicated that although the subcritical Hopf bifurcation is necessary to create a stimulus range in which the system is bistable (i.e., in which quiescence or repetitive spiking are both possible), bursting also requires a slow process like spike-dependent adaptation to sweep the system back and forth across the bistable region, thus allowing hysteresis to manifest bursting; in other words, bursting requires a subcritical Hopf bifurcation and adaptation (Rho and Prescott, 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling work, supported by a citation.

claim: Insertion of a virtual adaptation current enabled bursting under conditions associated with repetitive spiking in all three cells tested.
source: To test this, we inserted a virtual adaptation current ('Materials and methods'). As expected, this enabled bursting under conditions associated with repetitive spiking in all three cells tested (Figure 2D) but had no effect in the same three cells under normal conditions with onset-only spiking (data not shown).
evidence: This is an experimental result.

claim: Virtual adaptation current had no effect in cells under normal conditions with onset-only spiking.
source: To test this, we inserted a virtual adaptation current ('Materials and methods'). As expected, this enabled bursting under conditions associated with repetitive spiking in all three cells tested (Figure 2D) but had no effect in the same three cells under normal conditions with onset-only spiking (data not shown).
evidence: This is an experimental result.

claim: Bursting would have co-developed with repetitive spiking and MPOs if adaptation currents had been present.
source: These data confirm that bursting would have co-developed with repetitive spiking and MPOs if adaptation currents had been present, and suggest that adaptation currents are upregulated after nerve injury (possibly as a compensatory measure) rather than existing occultly in naive neurons whose spiking is already transient.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Adaptation currents are upregulated after nerve injury rather than existing occultly in naive neurons.
source: These data confirm that bursting would have co-developed with repetitive spiking and MPOs if adaptation currents had been present, and suggest that adaptation currents are upregulated after nerve injury (possibly as a compensatory measure) rather than existing occultly in naive neurons whose spiking is already transient.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental results.

claim: In 8 neurons in which neither decreasing potassium conductance nor increasing sodium conductance was sufficient to produce repetitive spiking and MPOs, the combination was sufficient to produce hyperexcitability in 7 of them.
source: Our third prediction was that manipulations tested independently in predictions 1 and 2 could combine to reproduce neuropathic changes in excitability; indeed, in 8 neurons in which neither decreasing potassium conductance nor increasing sodium conductance was sufficient to produce repetitive spiking and MPOs, we tested the two manipulations together and found that the combination was sufficient to produce hyperexcitability in 7 of them (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental result confirming a prediction.

claim: The minimum virtual sodium conductance needed to reproduce neuropathic excitability was reduced during 4-AP application.
source: We also observed that the minimum virtual sodium conductance needed to reproduce neuropathic excitability was reduced during 4-AP application (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The median virtual sodium conductance required for conversion was significantly reduced from 0.51 nS/pF without 4-AP to 0.23 nS/pF with 4-AP.
source: The median (and 25–75 percentile range) virtual sodium conductance was significantly reduced from 0.51 (range 0.47–0.63) nS/pF without 4-AP to 0.23 (range 0.13–0.40) nS/pF with 4-AP (p<0.001; Mann–Whitney U test) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental results.

claim: Hyperexcitability caused by blockade of native potassium conductance by 4-AP was reversed by insertion of virtual potassium conductance in 3 of 3 neurons tested.
source: To test this, we first tested whether inserting a virtual potassium conductance could reverse the hyperexcitability induced by blockade of native potassium conductance by 4-AP. Results confirmed our prediction in 3 of 3 neurons tested (Figure 3D), thus demonstrating the specificity of the 4-AP effect; in other words, even if channels other than Kv1 were blocked by 4-AP, the effect of 4-AP on excitability is attributable to blockade of subthreshold potassium current given that reintroducing that type of current reverses the altered excitability.
evidence: This is an experimental result.

claim: The effect of 4-AP on excitability is attributable to blockade of subthreshold potassium current.
source: To test this, we first tested whether inserting a virtual potassium conductance could reverse the hyperexcitability induced by blockade of native potassium conductance by 4-AP. Results confirmed our prediction in 3 of 3 neurons tested (Figure 3D), thus demonstrating the specificity of the 4-AP effect; in other words, even if channels other than Kv1 were blocked by 4-AP, the effect of 4-AP on excitability is attributable to blockade of subthreshold potassium current given that reintroducing that type of current reverses the altered excitability.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Hyperexcitability caused by insertion of a virtual sodium conductance was reversed by insertion of a virtual potassium conductance in 3 of 3 neurons tested.
source: More interesting is the observation that hyperexcitability caused by insertion of a virtual sodium conductance was reversed by insertion of a virtual potassium conductance in 3 of 3 neurons tested (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an experimental result.

claim: Only 1 of 9 injured cutaneous afferents exhibited any degree of repetitive spiking.
source: Surprisingly, only 1 of 9 injured cutaneous afferents exhibited any degree of repetitive spiking defined here as at least three spikes during sustained stimulation, which is not a significant change compared to chance (p=0.28; Fisher's exact test compared to spontaneous conversion rate of 0 in 23 cutaneous afferents).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: 6 of 9 injured neurons not labeled by intradermal injection of DiI exhibited neuropathic excitability.
source: By comparison, 6 of 9 injured neurons not labeled by intradermal injection of DiI exhibited neuropathic excitability, an example of which is shown in Figure 4A (p<0.001; Fisher's exact test compared to 1 in 9 cutaneous).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Muscle afferents are more prone than cutaneous afferents to becoming grossly hyperexcitable.
source: However, because the identity of unlabeled neurons is uncertain and given previous studies showing that muscle afferents are in fact more prone than cutaneous afferents to becoming grossly hyperexcitable (Michaelis et al., 2000; Liu et al., 2002), we retrogradely labeled muscle afferents.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 11 of 20 injured muscle afferents exhibited neuropathic excitability.
source: 11 of 20 injured muscle afferents exhibited neuropathic excitability (Figure 4B), which is a significantly higher proportion than 1 in 9 injured cutaneous afferents (p<0.05; Fisher's exact test) and the spontaneous conversion rate of 0 in 27 muscle afferents from naive animals (p<0.001; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Neuropathic excitability was reversed by insertion of virtual potassium conductance in 10 of 10 neurons tested.
source: Neuropathic excitability was reversed by insertion of virtual potassium conductance in 10 of 10 neurons tested or by reduction of sodium conductance via application of 10 µM riluzole in 4 of 4 neurons tested, thus confirming predictions 5 and 6, respectively (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental result confirming a prediction.

claim: Neuropathic excitability was reversed by reduction of sodium conductance via application of 10 µM riluzole in 4 of 4 neurons tested.
source: Neuropathic excitability was reversed by insertion of virtual potassium conductance in 10 of 10 neurons tested or by reduction of sodium conductance via application of 10 µM riluzole in 4 of 4 neurons tested, thus confirming predictions 5 and 6, respectively (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental result confirming a prediction.

claim: The median conductance needed to reverse neuropathic excitability in injured muscle afferents was only 0.14 nS/pF.
source: In the injured muscle afferents whose neuropathic excitability was reversed by insertion of virtual potassium conductance, the median conductance (and 25–75 percentile range) needed to cause reversal was only 0.14 (range 0.12–0.15) nS/pF.
evidence: This is an experimental result.

claim: The neuropathic state lies close to the tipping point.
source: This suggests that the neuropathic state lies close to the tipping point, which is consistent with our 100% success rate in reversing neuropathic excitability by manipulating either potassium or sodium conductance (see above).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Injured cutaneous afferents required significantly less virtual sodium conductance than uninjured cutaneous afferents to reach criticality.
source: In the four injured cutaneous afferents to which we added virtual sodium conductance, only 0.30 (range 0.14–0.44) nS/pF of sodium conductance was required to reproduce neuropathic excitability, which is significantly less than the 0.51 (range 0.47–0.63) nS/pF required to reproduce neuropathic excitability in uninjured cutaneous afferents (p<0.05; Mann–Whitney test) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Nerve injury leads to qualitatively altered excitability in only a subset of cells (ones that cross their tipping point) but the remaining cells are nonetheless quantitatively more excitable (closer to their tipping point).
source: Hence, nerve injury leads to qualitatively altered excitability in only a subset of cells (i.e., ones that cross their tipping point) but the remaining cells are nonetheless quantitatively more excitable (i.e., closer to their tipping point).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Muscle afferents from naive rats normally exhibit onset-only spiking.
source: Using neurons from naive rats, we subsequently verified that muscle afferents, like cutaneous afferents described in Figure 2, normally exhibit onset-only spiking (n = 27 muscle afferents).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Neuropathic excitability was reproduced in 16 of 20 muscle afferents by insertion of virtual sodium conductance.
source: Neuropathic excitability was reproduced in 16 of 20 muscle afferents by insertion of virtual sodium conductance (Figure 5A), which is a significantly greater conversion rate than 9 of 19 cutaneous afferents (p<0.05; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: The median sodium conductance required to reproduce neuropathic excitability was 0.31 nS/pF in muscle afferents compared with 0.51 nS/pF in cutaneous afferents.
source: Moreover, we found that the median sodium conductance required to reproduce neuropathic excitability was 0.31 (range 0.25–0.41) nS/pF in muscle afferents compared with 0.51 (range 0.47–0.63) nS/pF in cutaneous afferents, indicating that naive muscle afferents are significantly closer to their tipping point than naive cutaneous afferents (p<0.001; Mann–Whitney test) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Naive muscle afferents are significantly closer to their tipping point than naive cutaneous afferents.
source: Moreover, we found that the median sodium conductance required to reproduce neuropathic excitability was 0.31 (range 0.25–0.41) nS/pF in muscle afferents compared with 0.51 (range 0.47–0.63) nS/pF in cutaneous afferents, indicating that naive muscle afferents are significantly closer to their tipping point than naive cutaneous afferents (p<0.001; Mann–Whitney test) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Input resistance did not differ significantly between cutaneous and muscle afferents.
source: But notably, input resistance did not differ significantly between cutaneous and muscle afferents (p=0.2; unpaired t test; 282 ± 47 MΩ in cutaneous afferents vs 377 ± 57 MΩ in muscle afferents).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Muscle afferents are more prone to developing neuropathic excitability after nerve injury because they operate closer to their tipping point than do cutaneous afferents.
source: Overall, these data suggest that muscle afferents are more prone to developing neuropathic excitability after nerve injury because they operate closer to their tipping point than do cutaneous afferents.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: 4-AP and dendrotoxin produced repetitive spiking in only 1 of 12 muscle afferents.
source: We also tested whether neuropathic excitability could be reproduced in muscle afferents by reduction of potassium conductance by application or 4-AP or α-dendrotoxin. Contrary to the expectations, 4-AP and dendrotoxin reproduced neuropathic excitability in only 1 of 12 muscle afferents, which is a significantly lower conversion rate than 8 of 15 cutaneous afferents (p<0.05; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: The sustained outward current activated at perithreshold voltages and blocked by 10 nM dendrotoxin was significantly smaller in muscle afferents than in cutaneous afferents.
source: As predicted, the sustained outward current activated at perithreshold voltages (−50 mV to −30 mV) and blocked by 10 nM dendrotoxin was significantly smaller in muscle afferents than in cutaneous afferents (p<0.01; two-way ANOVA and post-hoc Student-Newman-Keuls test; 1.7 ± 0.6 pA/pF in muscle afferents vs 4.2 ± 0.6 pA/pF in cutaneous afferents after removing variance attributable to voltage) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Significantly less sodium conductance was needed to reproduce neuropathic excitability in muscle afferents with 4-AP than without 4-AP.
source: However, amongst muscle afferents in which neuropathic excitability was not reproduced by application of 4-AP and in which virtual sodium conductance was subsequently inserted, significantly less sodium conductance was needed to reproduce neuropathic excitability with 4-AP (0.22, range 0.14–0.27 nS/pF) than without 4-AP (0.31, range 0.25–0.41 nS/pF) (p<0.05; Mann–Whitney U test) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: 4-AP moves muscle afferents toward their tipping point but not far enough to reach it.
source: This indicates that 4-AP moves muscle afferents toward their tipping point but simply not far enough to reach it, reminiscent of the effects of nerve injury on cutaneous afferents (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: The relatively low expression of Kv1 channels in muscle afferents likely contributes to them existing closer to their tipping point.
source: Moreover, although many factors contribute to regulating excitability ('Introduction'), the relatively low expression of Kv1 channels in muscle afferents likely contributes to them existing closer to their tipping point, as shown in Figure 5B.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Primary afferent hyperexcitability associated with neuropathic pain arises through a switch in spike initiation dynamics that occurs when neurons cross a tipping point.
source: Using computer simulations and experiments, we have demonstrated that primary afferent hyperexcitability associated with neuropathic pain arises through a switch in spike initiation dynamics that occurs when neurons cross a tipping point.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: There are many different ways to cross the tipping point that separates normal and neuropathic excitability.
source: Furthermore, there are many different ways to cross that tipping point.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Criticality and degeneracy are fundamentally important concepts for understanding how complex systems fail, and how to therapeutically intervene to prevent or reverse those failures.
source: Criticality and degeneracy are fundamentally important concepts for understanding how complex systems fail, and how to therapeutically intervene to prevent or reverse those failures.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Treatment strategies for neuropathic pain must move away from single-target-drugs and towards a systems-based approach.
source: Our theory suggests that treatment strategies for neuropathic pain must move away from single-target-drugs and towards a systems-based approach, capitalizing on degeneracy rather than being thwarted by it.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings.

claim: Neuropathic symptoms often develop at long and highly variable delays after the inciting injury or disease.
source: For instance, neuropathic symptoms often develop at long and highly variable delays after the inciting injury or disease.
evidence: This is a clinical observation.

claim: Criticality can explain why neuropathic symptoms develop at long and variable delays after injury.
source: Criticality can explain this insofar as underlying molecular changes can develop occultly, without obvious outward manifestations, until a tipping point is reached, whereupon symptoms develop abruptly because of gross changes in excitability.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the concept of criticality.

claim: Once near the tipping point, symptoms could wax or wane because of the system moving forward and backward across its tipping point due to subtle fluctuations in underlying factors.
source: Furthermore, once near the tipping point, symptoms could wax or wane because of the system moving forward and backward across its tipping point due to subtle fluctuations in underlying factors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the concept of criticality.

claim: The homeostatic regulation of excitability may itself be deranged, maintaining the system at an incorrect 'set point' and hijacking degeneracy to paradoxically maintain hyperexcitability.
source: One possible explanation is that the homeostatic regulation of excitability is itself deranged, in effect maintaining the system at an incorrect 'set point' and hijacking degeneracy to paradoxically maintain hyperexcitability.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the difficulty in treating neuropathic pain.

claim: Therapeutically manipulating only one misregulated conductance will fail to sustainably reverse hyperexcitability if a deranged homeostatic control mechanism can fall back on other conductances.
source: In that scenario, therapeutically manipulating only one misregulated conductance will fail to sustainably reverse hyperexcitability if a deranged homeostatic control mechanism can fall back on other conductances to achieve its misguided goal.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the hypothesis about deranged homeostatic regulation.

claim: Multi-target drugs tend to work well for epilepsy.
source: If epilepsy has a similarly degenerate molecular basis (Klassen et al., 2011), it is no wonder that multi-target drugs tend to work well or that polypharmacy with single-target drugs is beneficial (Kwan et al., 2001); indeed, combination pharmacotherapy also offers benefits in the treatment of neuropathic pain (Chaparro et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Polypharmacy with single-target drugs is beneficial for epilepsy.
source: If epilepsy has a similarly degenerate molecular basis (Klassen et al., 2011), it is no wonder that multi-target drugs tend to work well or that polypharmacy with single-target drugs is beneficial (Kwan et al., 2001); indeed, combination pharmacotherapy also offers benefits in the treatment of neuropathic pain (Chaparro et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Combination pharmacotherapy offers benefits in the treatment of neuropathic pain.
source: If epilepsy has a similarly degenerate molecular basis (Klassen et al., 2011), it is no wonder that multi-target drugs tend to work well or that polypharmacy with single-target drugs is beneficial (Kwan et al., 2001); indeed, combination pharmacotherapy also offers benefits in the treatment of neuropathic pain (Chaparro et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Neuropathic pain may reflect the maladaptive homeostatic response to injury rather than being a direct consequence of injury.
source: The idea that neuropathic pain reflects the maladaptive homeostatic response to injury rather than being a direct consequence of injury has started to gain traction (Costigan et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Nerve injury induces numerous molecular changes within primary afferents.
source: In contrast to our simplified testing paradigm, nerve injury induces numerous molecular changes within primary afferents as evidenced by gene expression profiling (Costigan et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2002; Valder et al., 2003; Hammer et al., 2010; LaCroix-Fralish et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to gene expression profiling studies.
